analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum wages by region based on local living costs, rising to half the national average wage.
analysis.headline: The bill never left its first committee stop, and it died without a House vote when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the flat federal minimum wage with a regional one: each metro area or state's rural counties would get a wage set as a percentage of the national average hourly wage for non-supervisory private-sector workers, adjusted up or down for local price levels. It would start at 40% of that average, rise to 45% after a year and 50% after two years, and the wage could never go down from there. It would also raise the minimum cash wage for tipped workers to 30% of the local figure, and raise the special lower wage employers may pay to workers 18 and under.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers, especially in expensive metro areas where the local wage floor would be highest (roughly $16-17 an hour at full phase-in, versus the current $7.25 federal floor), plus tipped workers, whose required cash wage would jump from $2.13 to about 30% of the local minimum. In lower-cost rural areas the floor would be set lower, around $12-13 at full phase-in, still well above today's federal minimum.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage and tipped workers in high-cost areas

how_it_helps.text: Each metropolitan area and each state's rural counties would get a minimum wage set at a percentage of the national average hourly wage for non-supervisory private-sector workers, adjusted for regional price levels, starting at 40% and rising to 50% within two years, and never declining afterward.
The minimum cash wage for tipped employees would rise from the frozen $2.13 to 30% of the local determined wage, shrinking the gap employers can shift onto customers' tips.

The special subminimum wage for newly hired young workers would rise from $4.25 to two-thirds of the local minimum, and the reduced-wage window would be limited to workers 18 and under for 90 days instead of stretching to age 20.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay at or near the minimum wage — restaurants and other food service (especially those using the tipped credit), retail, agriculture, and care work — would face higher payroll costs, which they could meet through higher prices, reduced hours, automation, or absorbed margins.

drawbacks.text: The regional formula deliberately sets lower floors in low-cost areas — as little as 87.5% of the base in the cheapest places — so a worker doing the same job would be legally paid less depending on geography, and low-cost rural areas would never reach the same floor as big coastal metros.
The bill keeps a tipped subminimum wage in place (at 30% of the local figure) rather than eliminating it, so tipped workers would still depend on tips making up the remainder.

Higher mandatory wages are a real cost to small and low-margin employers, and critics of minimum wage increases generally argue the burden can fall on workers through reduced hours or hiring, particularly in regions where the floor rises fastest relative to local pay levels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A large, direct pay raise for the workers at the very bottom — millions earn under $12 an hour — versus real but diffuse costs spread across employers and prices. The design choice to vary the floor by local cost of living reduces the risk of job losses in cheap regions but also means the poorest counties get the smallest raise. It is a moderate, cost-of-living-aware version of a federal minimum wage increase rather than a single high national number.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) introduced the bill on December 12, 2023, with Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez as its one cosponsor, making the sponsorship bipartisan from the start.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day, and the committee took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
It remained in committee for the rest of the 118th Congress and expired on January 3, 2025, without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum or near-minimum wages — particularly restaurants using the tipped credit and other low-wage industries — avoided the higher payroll costs the bill would have imposed. Low-wage workers received no raise; the federal minimum remains $7.25.

industries.note: The bill would cut the tipped cash minimum from $2.13 to 30% of the local determined wage, directly reducing the wage subsidy tipped employers receive from customers' tips. It would also raise the base wage many restaurant workers are paid.

industries.industry: Retail, agriculture, and other minimum-wage employers
industries.note: Employers paying at or near the current $7.25 floor would owe significantly higher wages at full phase-in, with the largest increases in high-cost metros.
Not an industry, but the affected constituency: workers earning under the new regional floors would see mandated pay increases phased in over two years.
